title: When to relax a lockdown? A modelling-based study of testing-led strategies coupled with sero-surveillance against SARS-CoV-2 infection in India
abstract: India's lockdown against SARS-CoV-2, if lifted without any other mitigations in place, could risk a second wave of infection. A test-and-isolate strategy, using PCR diagnostic tests, could help to minimise the impact of this second wave. Meanwhile, population-level serological surveillance can provide valuable insights into the level of immunity in the population. Using a mathematical model, consistent with an Indian megacity, we examined how seroprevalence data could guide a test-and-isolate strategy, for lifting a lockdown. For example, if seroprevalence is 20% of the population, we show that a testing strategy needs to identify symptomatic cases within 5 - 8 days of symptom onset, in order to prevent a resurgent wave from overwhelming hospital capacity in the city. This estimate is robust to uncertainty in the effectiveness of the lockdown, as well as in immune protection against reinfection. To set these results in their economic context, we estimate that the weekly cost of such a PCR-based testing programme would be less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss due to the lockdown. Our results illustrate how PCR-based testing and serological surveillance can be combined to design evidence-based policies, for lifting lockdowns in Indian cities and elsewhere.

summary.oneLiner: A COVID-19 model suggests seroprevalence data can guide how quickly symptomatic cases must be tested and isolated when an Indian megacity lifts its lockdown.
summary.overview: The authors built a mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 spread in an Indian megacity to ask when a lockdown can safely be lifted. They find that if about 20% of the population already has immunity, symptomatic cases must be identified and isolated within roughly 5 to 8 days of symptom onset to keep a resurgent wave from overwhelming hospitals. They also estimate that a PCR testing programme of this kind would cost less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss from the lockdown, though they call this an upper bound. The paper frames serological surveys as a way to tell how intense testing needs to be.
summary.question: How can seroprevalence (the share of the population with antibodies) guide a PCR-based test-and-isolate strategy for lifting a lockdown without overwhelming hospital capacity, and how does its cost compare with the economic loss from the lockdown?
summary.method: A compartmental, deterministic transmission model stratified into three age groups, applied to a megacity akin to India. The authors simulated lifting a lockdown with no other interventions, and with an intensive two-pronged programme of RT-PCR testing and laboratory-based sero-surveillance started two weeks before lifting. They sampled across uncertain lockdown effectiveness and timing, asymptomatic transmission, and immunity against reinfection. Economic loss was estimated from sectoral productivity losses, and testing cost used an activity-based costing approach.
summary.data: No empirical patient or case dataset is described. The model is calibrated to illustrative scenarios for a megacity similar to Delhi, with R0 assumed between 2 and 3. Economic estimates use the state of Delhi's sectoral composition as an illustrative example. The paper is a preprint dated 2020 and uses no time period beyond the lockdown that began on 25 March 2020.
findings: If seroprevalence is 20% at the point of lifting the lockdown, symptomatic cases must be identified and isolated within 5 to 8 days of symptom onset to prevent a resurgent epidemic from overwhelming hospital capacity.
The authors state this estimate is robust to uncertainty in lockdown effectiveness and in immune protection against reinfection.

At R0 = 3 and 20% seroprevalence, symptomatic-only testing would need to identify cases within 2.5 to 4 days; the authors say this may be infeasible, so asymptomatic infections would need to be included.
Adding efforts to isolate half of asymptomatic infections reduces the required speed of symptomatic testing to 7 to 8 days at 20% seroprevalence with R0 = 3.

Productivity loss from the lockdown is estimated at 58% to 83.4%, or $1372 to $1979 million per week; the symptom-based testing programme is estimated at $26.68 to $42.12 million per week, which the authors say is an upper bound.
The authors suggest the testing cost is less than 2.1% of the weekly economic loss and less than half of the lockdown-caused loss in GST revenue.
The authors note that wider measures such as distancing in shops and transport would be expected to lower the testing intensity needed, but this is not modelled.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors argue that serological surveillance can inform how intensive test-and-isolate efforts must be before a lockdown is lifted, and that the testing cost they estimate is small relative to lockdown losses. They frame the work as evidence for policymakers in Indian cities and elsewhere. They also caution that the cost figures are an upper bound, that productivity loss ignores long-run demand effects, and that the model is illustrative rather than a forecast.
